title: The Mouth of a Lion That Was Never There
logline: The stairway to the top of a rock begins between two colossal masonry paws and climbs through the open mouth of a lion that was never an animal and is now not even a lion, and on the polished wall below it six centuries of visitors scratched names for painted figures nobody has ever been able to identify.
human_question: If the way up is named after an animal that never existed, and the figures on the cliff have been given a different name by everyone who ever looked at them, how much of what I am certain I am looking at did I bring with me?

place.what_kind_of_place: A single mass of hardened magma standing about a hundred and eighty metres clear of a flat dry-zone plain, carrying the ruins of a fifth-century royal citadel on it and around it. At the foot, symmetrical walled water gardens with fountains that still run in the rains; above them a belt of house-sized boulders and drip-ledged caves; then a stepped route up the western flank that runs out onto a gallery cut and built along the cliff, past a long wall of burnished lime plaster, past a rock shelter holding painted female figures, and onto a terrace halfway up where two colossal brick-and-masonry paws flank the start of the summit stairway and nothing at all stands above them. The summit is a few acres of brick foundations, cut cisterns and wind. A second, lower rock about a kilometre to the north, with a ruined monastery and a rough scramble to the top, gives the only ground-level position that holds the whole mass in one frame. It is one of the most visited places in the country, the route is single-file for much of its length, and the cliff carries large colonies of wild bees.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Four frames carry it with the sound off, and three of them need no aircraft. The whole rock from the lower rock opposite at first light, standing out of ground mist with the plain going on behind it and nothing else of that height anywhere in the frame. The gallery: a walkway and a spiral stair bolted to a vertical face, with the plain a long way below and the plastered wall running away along the rock. The wall itself, close in: a surface still glossy enough in places to give back a shape, and all over it thin stylus scratches in a script most viewers cannot read, held now behind a rail. And the paws terrace, which is the shot the film is built around: two masonry forelegs each about the length of a man, a flight of steps between them, and above them empty air where a head used to be, so that a camera tilting up from the steps passes straight through the missing animal and onto bare rock.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The light rotates onto the western flank through the afternoon and comes off it at dusk, which is when the cliff, the gallery and the paws are all lit from the same side. Mist lies on the plain in the hour after opening and burns off. Monsoon cloud comes over the summit and takes the view away in minutes. The crowd is the other clock: the route fills from opening, packs at the paws where the stair narrows, and thins again late in the day. And the bees move on their own schedule; the site asks visitors to keep quiet under the overhangs and keeps shelters on the path, and a colony lifting is a real event that stops everything.
place.when_it_looks_best: The drier months, when the plain is clear and the afternoon face holds its light. Within the day, two windows: the first hour, from the rock opposite, for mist and low sun on the west face and the smallest crowd of the day; and the last hours on the rock itself, when the light comes round onto the gallery and the paws. The wall needs raking side light to show the scratches at all, which means a narrow window and no flash. After heavy rain the gardens hold water and the fountains run, which is the only time the foot of the rock reads as it was built.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A climb film, dark to dusk, built on one of the strangest man-made objects anywhere. It opens across a gap at first light with a rock coming out of mist, walks in through flooded gardens and a field of boulders, goes up onto a walkway pinned to a cliff, passes a mirror-polished wall covered in a thousand years of handwriting and a pocket of rock with painted women in it, comes out between two enormous stone paws with a staircase running up between them into nothing, and finishes on a windy summit of foundations and cisterns before the light goes. It has a beginning, a climb and an ending and needs no narration at all.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the sources' argument about names, made on a site where the argument already happened by itself. The voice points only at what is on screen. The hill is named after an animal; the animal was brick, timber and plaster laid on rock, and it is gone, so the name now rests on nothing twice over. The wall below carries six centuries of visitors supplying names to painted figures that nobody since has been able to identify, and the film does not identify them either. And the wall is the sources' own distinction standing up in physical form: every one of those verses was once a sound, and the sound was the only part of it the books count as ultimately real, and the sound is gone, while the names, which were never in the air at all, are still in the plaster.

sequence.on_screen: First light from the summit of the lower rock across the gap. Ground camera, long lens and wide. The great rock stands out of mist on the plain, the west face still blue, no other high ground anywhere in frame.
sequence.voice: The name of this rock is the name of an animal. It has been called that for fifteen hundred years, in the chronicles, on the tickets, by everyone who lives under it. No lion ever lived here. The name did not come from an animal. It came from something people built.

sequence.on_screen: Walking in at ground level through the water gardens: straight-sided pools, fountain jets running after rain, the boulder field beyond, and the whole mass of rock filling the top of the frame.
sequence.voice: The books that this film is about treat a name as a thing in its own right, with a job. A name is what makes something known, and it is also the thing that gets made known — both at once, they say. The chronicle says King Kassapa had his gateways built in the fashion of lion faces, and the hill took the animal's name from the gateway. A door was named after a beast, and then a mountain was named after the door.

sequence.on_screen: Up on the gallery. The walkway and its spiral stair bolted to the vertical face; then the long wall alongside it, a curved plastered surface running away down the cliff, glossy where the light hits it, a rail in front of it.
sequence.voice: This wall was plastered and burnished until it gave back a reflection, and then people wrote on it. Not priests and not officials only — visitors, for something like eight hundred years, scratching verses into the polish with a metal point. Over a thousand of them have been recorded, and by one count more than eighteen hundred. It is the oldest visitors' book in the world, and it is still legible.

sequence.on_screen: Close on the plaster: thin stylus lines in a script the camera cannot read, crossing each other, some shallow enough to be light rather than mark. Then a slow tilt up the cliff to the rock shelter above the wall.
sequence.voice: Most of these verses are addressed upward, to the painted figures in the shelter above. And every writer gave them a name. Clouds and lightning, said one scholar. Apsaras, said another. Queens. Ladies of a court walking to a temple with flowers. Twenty-two figures survive, and in fifteen hundred years nobody has settled who they are, and this film is not going to settle it either.

sequence.on_screen: The painted pocket of rock from the permitted position, no flash: colour on plaster, and around it the bare grey cliff where the rest of the painted surface has gone, with the hard edge where plaster stops and rock begins.
sequence.voice: Here is what is actually on that rock. Pigment on plaster. The books count colour among the things that are really there, and they would say the same about the sound of your own breathing on these steps. What is not in that category is anything laid on top of it: whose wife, whose goddess, whose court. The colour has outlasted every name six hundred years of visitors gave it, and most of the colour is gone too.

sequence.on_screen: Back along the wall. A line of people passing behind the rail, voices moving along the gallery and away around the curve of the rock until only the wall and the scratches are left in frame.
sequence.voice: The books make a distinction here that is easy to miss and is exactly what this wall is. A sound is a real event: it starts, it arrives, it stops. The name is not the sound. The name is what comes up in whoever is listening. Every verse on this wall was once said out loud by somebody standing where you are standing. The sounds have gone, and they were the only part the books call ultimately real. The names were never in the air. What is left is scratches in plaster.

sequence.on_screen: The paws terrace. Two colossal brick-and-masonry forelegs, claws worn round, a flight of limestone steps starting between them. The camera comes up the steps and tilts, and the tilt passes through open sky where a head should be and lands on blank rock face.
sequence.voice: You go up between the paws. They are brick and cut stone, and they are all that is left of a gateway built as a lion — a head and a chest of timber, masonry and plaster laid against the rock, with the stair running up inside it. Whether climbers went in through the mouth or up a spiral within the body is still argued. Either way the way in was named after part of an animal. There was never an animal. Now there is not even a lion.

sequence.on_screen: The last stair up the open rock above the paws, then the summit: brick foundations, a cut cistern, wind. Then the reverse angle again at dusk, from the lower rock, the whole mass going dark.
sequence.voice: The books keep a category for a name like this one, and their own example is a king's son. Say it, and there is no king in it and no son in it either — a name resting on a name, and nothing underneath. The mouth of a lion. Everyone who has climbed this rock for fifteen hundred years has used it, none of them was wrong, and it has told every one of them exactly where to put their feet.

concept_merge.why_together: This idea carries C084 alone, and the digest is what makes one concept sufficient rather than thin. Read fresh, C084 is not a single point about language but a piece of machinery with several moving parts, and this site happens to have built most of them. Paññatti is defined as both what is made known and what makes it known [C084-P:L25], and the name-concept is defined as the name applied either to ultimates or to the meaning-concepts [C084-P:L47]. Among the meaning-concepts the sources list the concept of a being, whose examples include animals as well as people [C084-P:L33; C084-M:L17], and a lion is exactly that kind of item. The Margaya then supplies two things no analogy could: first, that a meaning-concept is what arises in the hearer's mind on the word, and that it arises through what the eye sees as well as through what is said [C084-M:L9]; second, the separation of the spoken sound, which is a paramattha dhamma, from the name it conveys, which is not, with the insistence that the name is not in the sounds at all but comes up in the listener [C084-M:L21]. Finally the sixfold sorting of name-concepts [C084-M:L23–L35; C084-P:L49–L71] includes the case where a name takes something not ultimately there as its basis and conveys something not ultimately there either, the sources' own examples being a king's son and a boy-son [C084-P:L71; C084-M:L35]. 'The mouth of a lion' is that case, on a terrace, in brick. Adding a second concept would only dilute the fact that one concept already has a physical instance of every part of itself in one place.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the interesting case is not a thing with several names but a name with nothing under it, and that this is ordinary rather than exotic. The confirmed opening film of this group watches four living names work perfectly well on one mountain that is definitely there. This film goes one step further down: an animal that never existed, a sculptural body of it that existed and is gone, a name that survives both and still functions as a direction to walk in. Set beside that, the wall does the other half. The Margaya says a meaning-concept also arises from what the eye sees [C084-M:L9], and here is six hundred years of it: hundreds of visitors looking at the same pigment and each one writing down a different thing they saw. The two together close off the cheap conclusion, because what is really on the cliff is colour, which the sources explicitly count as ultimately existent [C084-M:L29], and the film ends with the names still working and nothing debunked.

concept_links.why: The digest's general definition — paññatti as both what is made known and what makes it known [C084-P:L25], with the name-concept being the name applied to ultimates or to the meaning-concepts [C084-P:L47] — is the whole subject of the site, because the hill's name descends from a gateway and the gateway's name from an animal. The concept of a being, whose listed examples run from gods and humans to elephants, horses and oxen [C084-P:L33; C084-M:L17], is the specific slot a lion occupies, and here the slot is empty twice: no animal, and no longer even the sculpture that stood in for one. The sixfold sorting of name-concepts [C084-M:L23–L35; C084-P:L49–L71] contains the exact case, where the basis is not ultimately existent and what is conveyed is not either, the sources' examples being a king's son and a boy-son [C084-P:L71; C084-M:L35]. The wall carries the two Margaya claims a camera can actually observe: that a meaning-concept arises in the one who receives it, through the eye as much as through speech [C084-M:L9], which is what hundreds of visitors did to the same painted figures; and that the sound is a paramattha dhamma while the name it conveys is not, the name being nowhere in the sounds and only arising in the listener [C084-M:L21], which is why a wall of scratches left by vanished speech is this concept in physical form. The digest's own limits are load-bearing and are written into the film. The film must never tell anybody that the name they use is wrong, so no beat corrects a guide, a pilgrim, a visitor or a scholar, and beat eight exists to say the opposite out loud. The existent and non-existent pairs are technical Abhidhamma categories and are never rendered as true and false or as fake: the voice says 'nothing underneath', never 'not real'. And the film must not overreach into 'language constructs reality' or 'nothing is real', which is why beat five stops on pigment and says the sources count colour among the things that are really there [C084-M:L29] before it says anything about names at all.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a name does not need anything underneath it in order to work, and that the names we are most certain of are often the ones we supplied ourselves. The proof needs no belief and is on screen twice: a staircase everybody climbs through the mouth of an animal that never existed, and a wall of people telling a painted surface who it was.
what_must_be_real: Every frame is the site as it is now: no reconstruction of the lion, no animated head restored over the paws, no composite that puts a face back on the rock, and no digital reading of the verses laid over the plaster. The absence is the subject and it is never filled in. The wall and the paintings are never touched, lit with flash, or filmed from anywhere other than the position visitors are permitted to stand in, and if photography of the painted shelter is refused on the day, the film says what it cannot show rather than obtaining it another way. Nobody on the route is an exhibit: the crowd appears as a crowd, from behind or wide, never as an identified person being characterised, and nobody is asked to pose, to climb again, or to look at anything twice. No shot is set up anywhere that blocks or slows the stairway, the gallery or the paws terrace, which are single-file and are the whole site's bottleneck; if a frame cannot be got without holding people up, it is not got. The verses are quoted only from published readings and are attributed as readings, not as settled text. The identity of the painted figures is left open in the voice and in the framing, and the figures are filmed as painting, never as bodies.
position_hint: second or third in the group, after the film that shows several working names on one real thing: this one takes the next step, to a name with nothing under it at all, and the group's later films on wholes, parts and emptiness stand on it. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Consent in a crowd. This is one of the busiest sites in the country and the route is single-file; nobody in frame can meaningfully refuse a camera on a stairway they cannot step off, so the crowd is filmed as a crowd and no identifiable person is ever presented as a character or an example.

Obstruction. A tripod or a stopped operator on the gallery, the spiral stair or the paws terrace is a safety problem before it is a discourtesy, and the best light is also the busiest hour. Shots that need the terrace clear may simply be unobtainable.

The painted figures. The voice must not be prurient, must not describe bodies, and must not settle who the figures are; the verses' amorous character is a historical fact about the writers and is not an invitation to the camera. Photographing the paintings has been restricted and flash is prohibited, so beat five may have to be carried by the plaster and the bare cliff alone.

Adjudicating the site's own history. The chronicle's account of how Kassapa came to the throne is deliberately not used: it is not needed for the concept, and a violent accession followed by a lost battle would invite exactly the reading of kamma as verdict that this project refuses. The film records layers and settles nothing.
Treating the sources' existent and non-existent pairs as 'true' and 'false' or as 'fake'; they are technical Abhidhamma categories, and a name for something that was never there is not thereby a lie.

Overreaching into 'language constructs reality' or 'nothing is real'. The digest keeps sound, colour, feeling and mind fully real and treats conventional wholes as valid in their own domain, which is why the film stops on pigment before it talks about names.
Telling anybody that the name they use is wrong. The digest forbids it outright, and the temptation here is strong because the film's own subject is a name with nothing under it.

Repeating the group's opening film. That film is four living names for one mountain that exists; this one must stay on a name for something that never existed and on names supplied by viewers, and must not drift into a comparison of traditions or a shadow.

Drone permission over a World Heritage site is genuinely doubtful and may be refused outright. The film is therefore built so that every load-bearing frame — the reverse angle, the gallery, the wall, the paws, the summit — is obtainable on foot.
Wild bee colonies on the overhangs. Attacks happen, the site asks for quiet, and drone noise or a raised voice near a colony is a hazard to everyone on the path, not just to the crew.

Becoming a heritage documentary. The history is the argument, not the content: the film is not about a king, a citadel or an archaeological controversy, and the moment the voice starts explaining the site it has lost its subject.
drop_if: Filming on the gallery, the wall or the paws terrace cannot be done without holding up a single-file route.
Access to the paws terrace with a camera, or to the wall at a raking-light hour, is refused, since the film has no second version of either shot.
The only way to show the lion is to reconstruct it.

connections.note: Four living names for one mountain that is unquestionably there, and then one ancient name for an animal that never was. That film records that it absorbed this idea's earlier strand, which was an abstract version of its own move; this rewrite shares nothing with it.
A whole that comes apart into its parts when you divide it, and a name whose thing was never assembled in the first place.

That film holds the sources' space-concept, a thing named by the emptiness in it, and this one deliberately leaves that category alone: the absent mouth is handled as a being-concept and a name resting on a name, not as a named hollow.

selection.reason: It is the group's film on a name with nothing under it, which is the step past the opening film, and the site supplies both halves of it as recorded history rather than as resemblance: a name descended from an absent sculpture, and six centuries of visitors naming figures nobody can identify.

suggested_location.name: Sigiriya (Sīhagiri, the Lion Rock), with Pidurangala opposite

also_known_as.name: Sīhagiri / Sinhagiri
also_known_as.meaning: lion rock; the chronicle derives it from gateways built in the fashion of lion faces
also_known_as.used_by: the Cūḷavaṃsa and Mahāvaṃsa tradition, and scholarly writing

also_known_as.name: Lion Rock
also_known_as.meaning: the English rendering in use on signage and tickets

also_known_as.name: Pidurangala
also_known_as.meaning: the lower rock and ruined monastery about a kilometre north, used here for the reverse angle

suggested_location.region: Matale District, Central Province; in the northern part of the district on the dry-zone plain between Dambulla and Habarane, with Pidurangala about a kilometre north of the main rock
suggested_location.elevation_note: The rock stands about 180 m above the surrounding plain; the summit is commonly given as around 349 m above sea level. Pidurangala opposite is roughly 195 m above the plain.
suggested_location.why_here: It is the one place where this concept's story is not an analogy but the recorded history of the site. The summit stairway begins between two colossal masonry paws which are all that survives of a gateway built as a lion, and the rock's own name is that animal, traced by the chronicle to the lion-faced gateway rather than to any beast — so the name rests on a sculpture that is gone of an animal that never existed, which is precisely the sources' category of a name whose basis is not ultimately there and whose object is not either. Directly below, the Mirror Wall holds six centuries of visitors' verses addressed to painted figures whose identity has never been agreed by anyone, which is the same concept from the other side: meaning arriving in whoever looks, and each looker writing down a different name for it. And it delivers the cinema in the same objects: a two-hundred-metre monolith out of mist, a walkway bolted to a cliff, a burnished wall covered in a thousand years of handwriting, and a staircase climbing between two paws into open air where a head used to be. Nowhere else in the country carries both the frame and this particular story.
what_to_film: The whole rock at first light from the summit of the lower rock opposite, on foot, with mist on the plain. This is the opening and the closing frame and it needs no aircraft, which is why the film can survive a drone refusal.
The approach at ground level through the water gardens after rain, when the pools hold water and the fountains run, with the rock filling the top of the frame.
The gallery: the walkway and the spiral stair pinned to the vertical face, shot along the cliff so the drop and the curve of the rock are both in frame.

The Mirror Wall in raking side light, wide enough to show it running away along the cliff and then close enough to show individual stylus scratches. Filmed from behind the rail, without contact and without flash.
The painted shelter from the permitted standing position, no flash: colour on plaster, and the bare cliff around it where the painted surface has gone, including the edge where plaster stops.

The paws terrace, which is the payoff: the two forelegs, the steps starting between them, and a tilt from the steps up through the empty air where the head and chest stood, landing on blank rock. Everything else is arranged around getting this clean.
The summit: brick foundations, a cut cistern, the plain in every direction, wind on the microphone.
The crowd as a crowd and as sound — feet on stone, voices moving along the gallery and away — never as identified individuals, and never in a way that requires anyone to stop.
suggested_location.access: A ticketed archaeological site with a single main entrance, open from early morning; the ascent is on masonry steps, iron staircases and a spiral stair on the cliff, and is single-file for much of its length. Photography of the paintings has been restricted and flash is prohibited; the Mirror Wall is behind a rail and may not be touched. Any professional filming needs permission from the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund, and a drone would additionally need the Civil Aviation Authority, the Ministry of Defence and local police, which for a World Heritage site of this profile is slow and may simply be refused. Pidurangala opposite is reached by a separate path through a monastery with a short rough scramble at the top, is not part of the same ticket, and is climbed in the dark for first light.
suggested_location.best_time: The drier months for a clear plain and a working afternoon light. Within the day: the first hour from Pidurangala for mist and low sun on the west face, and the last hours on the rock itself when the light comes round onto the gallery and the paws. The wall needs a narrow window of raking side light. The gardens only read as built when they hold water, which means shooting shortly after rain, and that is in tension with wanting a clear plain.

historical_thread.story: The citadel on the rock is attributed to Kassapa I, who reigned roughly 477–495 CE and was defeated by Moggallāna in 495. Halfway up the western flank, on the terrace where the summit stairway begins, stand two colossal paws of brick and cut masonry, each around three metres long. They are the surviving fragment of a monumental gateway built in the form of a lion. Senaka Bandaranayake's reading is that the figure comprised a head, chest and paws of timber, brick and plaster laid against the rock, with the stairway running up inside it; H. C. P. Bell, writing in 1898 of 'huge claws of a once gigantic lion', described a winding stair passing through the body, while the site authority's own account has climbers ascending through staircases that emerged from the beast's mouth. The head is gone and is thought to have stood at least into the ninth century. The rock's name is that animal: Sīhagiri, lion rock, which the chronicle derives not from any beast but from gateways 'built after the fashion of lion faces'. Below the terrace, a long wall of brick masonry faced in burnished lime plaster runs along the gallery. Visitors wrote on that polish with metal styluses: over eighteen hundred separate graffiti have been recorded, spanning by the site authority's account the sixth to the fourteenth centuries, of which Senarat Paranavitana published readings of 685 verses which he placed in the eighth to tenth centuries. Of the 685 identified writers, twelve were women. It is the oldest surviving visitors' book anywhere and among the oldest surviving Sinhala poetry. The great majority of the verses are addressed upward, to the painted female figures in the rock shelter above the wall, of which twenty-two survive out of a painted surface that once ran for something like a hundred and forty metres; one of the verses itself speaks of five hundred ladies in the paintings. Who the figures are has never been agreed. Paranavitana read them as cloud damsels and lightning princesses, personifications of cloud and lightning. Ananda Coomaraswamy read them as apsaras. H. C. P. Bell took them for ladies of the king's court carrying flowers to a temple. Others have read them as a queen with an attendant, or as women at a religious observance. Fifteen hundred years of visitors have supplied names, and no name has stuck.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C084's subject is the difference between what is made known and the means of making it known, and its hardest case is a name whose basis is not ultimately there and whose object is not either — the sources' own examples being a king's son and a boy-son. 'The mouth of a lion' is that case standing on a terrace. A lion belongs to the concept of a being, which the sources ground in the five aggregates and illustrate with animals as readily as with people; this lion had no aggregates at all, being brick, timber and plaster on rock, and now even that is gone, so the name has lost not only its animal but its substitute. The rock's name is that same animal, at one further remove: named from a gateway, which was named from a face, which was never a face. And the wall is the other half of the same concept in physical form. The Margaya says a meaning-concept arises in whoever receives it and arises through the eye as well as through the word, and it separates the spoken sound, which it calls a paramattha dhamma, from the name the sound conveys, which it does not — the name being nowhere in the syllables and only coming up in the listener. Every verse on that wall was a sound once. The sounds are gone; the names are still in the plaster; and the pigment they were all written about is colour, which the sources count among the things that really are there. The site did not illustrate this. It did it, for six hundred years, in writing, before anyone thought to film it.
historical_thread.what_is_certain: Two colossal paws of brick and masonry survive on the terrace where the summit stairway begins, each around three metres long, and they are all that remains of the gateway structure. The head does not survive. The site's name means lion rock. The Mirror Wall is brick masonry faced in highly polished lime plaster. Over eighteen hundred graffiti have been recorded on it; Paranavitana published readings of 685 verses. Twenty-two painted female figures survive in the shelter above the wall, from a painted area that was once far larger. Kassapa I's reign is placed at roughly 477–495 CE. The rock rises about 180 m above the plain.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed: Whether climbers passed through the lion's mouth or up a spiral stair within its body: the site authority says the mouth, Bell's 1898 account and Bandaranayake's reconstruction describe a stair through the figure. Whether the sculpture was a complete lion or only the forequarters — head, chest and paws — and how long the head stood. The extent and dating of the graffiti: the site authority gives the sixth to fourteenth centuries and more than 1,800 inscriptions, Paranavitana's published corpus is 685 verses of the eighth to tenth, and other counts run to 1,500 or beyond, many fragmentary. Who the painted figures are: cloud damsels and lightning princesses (Paranavitana), apsaras (Coomaraswamy), ladies of the court on their way to a temple (Bell), a queen with an attendant, or women at a religious observance. What the site was for — fortress, palace, or monastic complex — is also argued, as is the chronicle's account of how Kassapa came to the throne, which this film does not use.

suggested_location.research_note: The lion gateway and its surviving paws, the derivation of the name, the Mirror Wall's construction and graffiti counts and dating, the twenty-two surviving painted figures, the competing identifications, Kassapa I's dates and the heights and coordinates are all desk research from the sources above; the site authority's account and the scholarly accounts disagree on several points and those disagreements are recorded in historical_thread rather than smoothed over. Coordinates are the commonly cited point for the rock and for the lower rock opposite and have not been checked on the ground. Permissions are the main open question: professional filming needs the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund, aerial work needs the Civil Aviation Authority, the Ministry of Defence and local police as well, and a drone over a World Heritage site of this profile may well be refused; nothing here has been applied for. Reports that photographing the paintings has been prohibited, and that flash is banned and the wall may not be touched, are from the sources above and need confirming with the site authority as the rules stand now. Current opening hours, ticket conditions and the state of the bee colonies are unverified.

unknowns: No permission has been sought or confirmed. Filming permission from the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund, and the conditions attached to it, are entirely unverified.

Drone permission over a World Heritage site of this profile is genuinely uncertain and may be refused outright, and would in any case need the Civil Aviation Authority, the Ministry of Defence and local police as well as the heritage bodies. The film is built to survive a refusal: the reverse angle, the gallery, the wall, the paws and the summit are all obtainable on foot.

Whether the painted shelter may be filmed at all, and under what conditions, is unresolved; reports of a photography ban and a flash prohibition need confirming, and beat five may have to be carried without the figures.

Whether a camera can work on the gallery, the spiral stair and the paws terrace without holding up a single-file route, and whether an out-of-hours or low-season window exists, has not been established.

Whether raking side light reaches the plastered wall at a usable hour, and whether the scratches read on camera from behind the rail at the permitted distance, are unverified and the wall beats depend on both.
The state of the wild bee colonies, the site's current noise rules under the overhangs, and what they imply for recording sound or flying anything, are unknown.
Which published readings of the verses may be quoted, and on what terms, has not been checked.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Chathura's choice; its supporting history is desk research from published sources, with the disagreements between them recorded rather than resolved, and none of it is documentary evidence. No scene or shot is decided here; the sequence is a shape for the film, not a shot list.
